frameworks.name: Logic-Evidence-Utility Framework
frameworks.definition: A decision-filtering model: logic (what does it mean?), evidence (how do I know that?), utility (why should I care?). Only pursue questions or stressors that change behavior or outcomes.

claims.text: The meaning of life is the set of things that would stop you from taking your own life. When someone says they don't know the meaning of their life, the response 'well, why don't you kill yourself?' cuts directly to what actually matters—and that answer (family, purpose, impact) IS the meaning.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Observable consequences of action (staying alive for something) reveal true meaning; meaning is revealed through what you won't sacrifice, not through abstract philosophy.
bounded_by: Only applies as a definitional framework, not as actionable life guidance

claims.text: Meaning is entirely self-generated. You decide what is meaningful, and because of that you can create and destroy meaning as you see fit. Meaning does not have to be the same one thing for your entire life.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Apply a utility filter to every question or stressor: 'What does it mean (define precisely)? How do I know that (evidence)? Why should I care (does it change my behavior or outcomes)?' Only spend energy on things that pass the utility test—that demonstrably affect your life.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When deciding whether to pursue curiosity or address a stressor

claims.text: Most people get hung up on things that do not affect their reality. The binding constraint on success is not information gathering—it is ruthlessly eliminating non-load-bearing concerns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Questions like 'Are we in a simulation?' or 'What are unidentified anomalous phenomena?' should be scored on utility: if the answer doesn't change your behavior today, the question itself changes nothing. Zero curiosity should be directed toward low-utility mysteries.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When considering time investment in abstract philosophical or speculative questions
bounded_by: Does not apply to questions whose answers would demonstrably change behavior (e.g., if aliens were confirmed to exist and actively intervened, behavior would change)

claims.text: Stressed-out is not a feeling—it is a specific behavior or outcome triggered by a specific event. Define stress precisely (e.g., 'someone trolled me online'), then ask: how do you know it's true, and does it affect your life? If it doesn't change how you live, logically you should not care.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When addressing emotional states or stressors
claims.mechanism: Vague emotional labels (stressed, anxious, overwhelmed) are treated as problems until deconstructed into observable causes and measurable impacts; the majority dissolve under this scrutiny.

examples.text: Someone says 'I'm really stressed out.' The clarification process: 'What does stressed out mean to you?' They respond, 'Someone trolled me online.' Then: 'How do you know it was bad? How do you know it was about you? What did it affect?' At the end, the person realizes: 'It hasn't really changed anything.' Conclusion: logically, this event should not affect your emotional state or time allocation.

The question 'Are we in a simulation?' illustrates zero-utility curiosity. Even if true, it changes nothing about daily behavior—so zero effort is directed toward it. Only when an answer would demonstrably alter action (e.g., if aliens were found to be actively controlling behavior) would the question become load-bearing.

practices.text: When stuck on a hard decision or stressor, immediately ask: What does it mean (define it precisely)? How do I know that (what's the evidence)? Why should I care (does it change how I live or my outcomes)?
Build your reality by only including things that are ultimately necessary to the success of that reality; eliminate non-load-bearing information and concerns.
When asking 'What's the meaning of my life?', first answer 'Why don't I kill myself?' The things you would not sacrifice for—family, work, impact—are your actual meaning.
